recent_posts.title: Unfortunately, Sprites Now Speak MCP
recent_posts.summary: Fly.io has added MCP (Model Context Protocol) support to Sprites, their disposable cloud VM product, allowing AI agents like Claude, Gemini, and Codex to spin up and manage Sprites directly. The post is candid that MCP is not the preferred integration method — the team argues CLI tools and discoverable APIs are more efficient because they reveal capabilities progressively and avoid bloating agent context with unused tool descriptions. MCP is offered as a fallback for agents that can't run shell commands. The post also advocates for giving agents real computers with persistent filesystems over stateless sandboxes, and includes guardrails like org-scoped authentication, Sprite count caps, and name prefixes to keep agent-created VMs manageable.

recent_posts.title: How Sprites achieve durable storage without physical disks
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into how Sprites (hardware-isolated stateful sandboxes) achieve durable storage without physical disks. Starting from Linux file system basics, it explains how file systems like ext4 interact with block devices via BIO requests, how OverlayFS enables layered container file systems, and how the Network Block Device (NBD) protocol allows block IO to be handled by a user-space process instead of hardware. Sprites use this to run a process called SpriteFS that intercepts block-level reads/writes and stores data as chunks in object storage, with metadata in a SQLite database also synced to object storage — making sandboxes both disposable and persistent.

recent_posts.title: N-tier architecture is not your only option.
How Litestream solves SQLite durability with WAL replication
recent_posts.summary: SQLite's main weakness is durability—if your server dies, the database file goes with it. Litestream solves this by continuously replicating SQLite changes to object storage like S3. It works by controlling SQLite's write-ahead log (WAL) process: holding a read transaction open to prevent automatic checkpointing, copying WAL changes to a shadow directory, then uploading them to remote storage. Combined with periodic full snapshots, this enables database restoration elsewhere with minimal data loss, making SQLite viable for production backends on ephemeral infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: We made our sandboxes stateful – here's how.
recent_posts.summary: Sprites are stateful sandbox environments that combine VM persistence with container convenience. They use object storage for the entire filesystem, breaking file contents into chunks (blobs) stored remotely while keeping metadata in a local SQLite database backed by Litestream. This architecture enables sub-second checkpoint creation and restoration similar to Git commits. The system provides 100GB storage, root permissions, and continuous syncing, making it ideal for AI agents like Claude that need real computers rather than ephemeral containers. Sprites can be spun up in under a second and support quick rollbacks when experiments fail.

recent_posts.title: What are Sprites, and why does Claude love them?
Litestream Writable VFS
recent_posts.summary: Litestream VFS now supports write operations and background hydration for faster cold starts. The writable VFS mode buffers writes locally and syncs to object storage periodically, enabling single-writer scenarios with eventual durability. Background hydration pulls the full database from S3 while serving reads remotely, then switches to the local copy when ready. These features power Fly.io's Sprites storage stack, where every Sprite boots with 100GB of durable storage in under a second by using Litestream SQLite with S3-backed block maps.

recent_posts.title: Running stateful sandboxes in VS Code | VS Code + Sprites
recent_posts.summary: Sprites is a stateful sandbox environment for running AI-generated code, particularly with Claude AI pre-installed. A new VS Code extension allows developers to create, manage, and edit sprites directly from their editor. The demo shows creating a simple to-do app by opening a sprite terminal, running Claude to generate code, and editing the resulting files in VS Code while the app runs in the sandbox environment.

recent_posts.title: Building a web app with Fly.io Sprites and Claude AI
recent_posts.summary: Fly.io Sprites are stateful sandbox environments designed for running arbitrary code safely, perfect for experimentation and AI-assisted development. They feature checkpoint functionality that allows rolling back entire system states (beyond just code), making them ideal for exploratory work. The demo shows building a dog training tracker web app using Claude AI within a Sprite environment, leveraging built-in tools like GitHub CLI and the ability to create/restore checkpoints when things go wrong or to compare different approaches.

recent_posts.title: The Design & Implementation of Sprites
recent_posts.summary: Fly.io's new Sprites platform provides instant-creation Linux VMs with 100GB persistent storage that auto-sleep when idle. The architecture abandons container images for faster provisioning, uses S3-compatible object storage instead of attached NVMe for durability and mobility, and runs orchestration inside the VM rather than on the host. Sprites create in 1-2 seconds by pre-pooling standard containers, checkpoint/restore quickly via metadata operations, and integrate with Fly.io's existing Corrosion service discovery. The design trades some performance for dramatically simplified operations and enables disposable, ephemeral computing workflows.
